newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: OAU welcomes U.S. help to organise Africa force.
newsitem.headline: OAU welcomes U.S. help to organise Africa force.

text.p: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) welcomed on Monday a U.S. initiative to train and equip an African intervention force on the condition that it was not permanent.
The OAU was planning an emergency response force made up of national army detachments trained and equipped to respond immediately to crises, OAU spokesman Ibrahim Dagash said.
"The OAU may want to launch peacekeeping operations of a limited nature in exceptional circumstances and that is where the U.S. initiative is welcome," Dagash told Reuters.
"(But) it must be very clear from the outset that the OAU is not at all intending to have a permanent peacekeeping force and does not support a proposal to this effect," he said.

The Washington Post said on Saturday President Bill Clinton had approved an ambitious plan to organise, train, equip and help deploy an all-African force of 10,000 troops to intervene in African crises.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher was expected next week during his first trip to sub-Saharan Africa to discuss the African Crisis Response Force (ACRF) plan with African leaders.
Assistant Secretary of State for Africa George Moose toured Africa last week to solicit troop commitments from Zimbabwe, Botswana, Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya and Mozambique.
The Washington Post said the ACRF would be sent to countries where insurrection, civil war or campaigns of genocide threatened mass civilian casualties.
The ACRF would not intervene in the fighting but would establish and protect safe areas where civilians could gather and receive humanitarian assistance, according to the report.
U.S. officials estimate it would cost $25 million to set up the force and a further $40 million if the force was deployed.
The United States was prepared to pick up half the cost and was counting on European allies to come up with the rest in cash, equipment or training, officials told the Washington Post.
It said the force would be created only if the United States could get necessary support from African and European countries.
Senior OAU officials were working on their limited plan, which could dovetail with the U.S. initiative, Dagash said.
"The new U.S. initiatve would very much fall within the framework of the crisis response force which the OAU was planning to organise," he said.
"The OAU's position is that peacekeeping is exclusively the domain of the United Nations Security Council," Dagash said.
The OAU has resisted any proposal for a permanent crisis response force because of a lack of money and political differences between member states.
